# Vectors in Postgres

[pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) adds a `vector` type, four distance operators and
two index types to Postgres. With it, "find the passages most similar to this question" is an
`ORDER BY ... LIMIT`, and the embeddings sit in the same table as the text, the permissions and the
foreign keys. This chapter covers the query side; the next one compares the indexes.

## Four distances

| SQL | SQLAlchemy | what it is | index opclass |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a <-> b` | `col.l2_distance(b)` | Euclidean distance | `vector_l2_ops` |
| `a <=> b` | `col.cosine_distance(b)` | 1 minus the cosine: 0 same direction, 2 opposite | `vector_cosine_ops` |
| `a <#> b` | `col.max_inner_product(b)` | the negative inner product (so smaller is closer) | `vector_ip_ops` |
| `a <+> b` | `col.l1_distance(b)` | taxicab distance | `vector_l1_ops` |

For normalized embeddings, which most models produce, cosine and inner product rank identically,
and inner product skips a division. The notebook starts with a dozen hand-made three-dimensional
vectors whose axes mean something (`[fruit, tech, sport]`), so every distance can be predicted in
your head before Postgres computes it.

## Nearest neighbours

The core pattern, with everything else as decoration:

```python
distance = Document.embedding.cosine_distance(query_vec).label("distance")
stmt = (
    select(Document.title, distance)
    .where(Document.category == "orm")  # ordinary filters first
    .order_by(distance)
    .limit(5)
)
```

Two refinements come up in every real system. **Retrieve, then rerank**: take the top 50 by vector
distance in a CTE, then order those by a blended score (similarity and popularity, recency, a
cross-encoder). **Top-k per group**: `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY distance)`
and keep the first three of each.

## Upserting embeddings

Embedding pipelines re-run. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` on a unique key inserts new rows and
refreshes changed ones in one statement:

```python
stmt = insert(Document).values(rows)
stmt = stmt.on_conflict_do_update(index_elements=["name"], set_={"embedding": stmt.excluded.embedding})
```

## An index changes the answer

With no index Postgres computes every distance and sorts: exact, and fine to some tens of thousands
of rows. An approximate nearest-neighbour index is much faster and *slightly wrong*, and how wrong
is a setting. Two rules that cost people hours:

::: {.callout-warning}
## The opclass must match the operator

An HNSW index built with `vector_l2_ops` is ignored by a query ordering by `<=>`. The plan quietly
goes back to a sequential scan. Check with `EXPLAIN` after every index change.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Filters run after the walk

HNSW collects `hnsw.ef_search` candidates and then applies `WHERE`. A filter that keeps 10% of rows
throws most candidates away, and the query can return fewer rows than its `LIMIT`. pgvector 0.8
added iterative scans that keep walking until the limit is met:
`SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order`.
:::

## The doc-search app

The lab's FastAPI app is this chapter in production form. `app/ingest.py` fetches 20 pages of the
SQLAlchemy documentation, chunks them by section (about 250 words), embeds each chunk with
`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` (384 dimensions, ONNX on the CPU) and stores 407 rows with an HNSW index.
`POST /ask` embeds a question, takes the top five chunks by cosine distance and builds an extractive
summary from their sentences, so nothing is generated and every answer carries its sources.
Retrieval takes about 20 ms. The [sync and async scene](sqlalchemy.qmd#watching-it-happen) shows
those queries in flight, with the chunks laid out by a PCA of their real embeddings.

covers all of the above plus the index comparison of the next chapter.
